title: AI may widen global and internal divergence when infrastructure, skills, institutions, and voice arrive unevenly
source_unit: United Nations Development Programme Regional Bureau for Asia and the Pacific, The Next Great Divergence: Why AI May Widen Inequality Between Countries
geography: Asia-Pacific, with country and within-country comparisons across different levels of income, digital readiness, institutional capacity, connectivity, skills, and gender equality; recommendations are presented as globally relevant

denominator.unit: regional human-development report covering Asia-Pacific countries and internal capability differences

central_risk.value: AI can produce a new divergence if gains concentrate among countries, cities, large firms, and highly skilled workers while lower-capacity places face weaker infrastructure, skills, and governance

transmission_channels.value: the report analyzes unequal AI effects through people, economy, and governance

starting_point_gap.value: countries and communities differ sharply in power, connectivity, skills, data, institutional capacity, and ability to absorb shocks

decision_window.value: current choices and safeguards are presented as shaping development trajectories for decades

observations.method: UNDP synthesis drawing on nine background papers, regional evidence, country comparisons, sector analysis, and policy roadmaps; it is a forward-looking human-development assessment rather than a causal forecast of AI effects.
observations.uncertainty: The report emphasizes substantial uncertainty about the scale and distribution of AI gains; regional diversity makes sweeping country-level conclusions inappropriate, and many impacts remain scenario-based or conditional.
observations.subgroup: Lower-capacity and remote communities, rural residents, women, informal and care workers, minorities, displaced people, small firms, routine workers, and countries with weak power, connectivity, data, or institutional systems.
observations.counterinterpretation: AI could allow latecomers to leapfrog through local-language education, health support, agricultural advice, disaster warning, and public-service access if foundational systems and safeguards are built inclusively.

observations.period: 2026; people, capability, security, and environmental pressure

capability_promise.value: AI could support local-language tutoring, clinical triage, social-protection targeting, disaster prediction, and environmental monitoring

exclusion_route.value: people and communities missing from data can become invisible to AI systems, while opaque or biased systems can deny credit, benefits, or rights

gender_exposure.value: women may face heightened exposure to algorithmic bias and online harm because of gender divides in digital access, informal work, and care economies

resource_cost.value: large AI systems consume energy and water, creating environmental and infrastructure burdens alongside potential benefits

observations.method: Human-development synthesis connecting AI applications to capability, security, rights, gender, data visibility, and environmental conditions.
observations.uncertainty: The report identifies plausible pathways and policy risks; it does not estimate a uniform effect of AI on health, education, benefits access, gender equality, or environmental outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Women and girls, rural and remote communities, elderly people, minorities, displaced people, people with weak digital access, and people dependent on public benefits or local services.
observations.counterinterpretation: The same systems that can exclude can also reduce distance and administrative burden when local data, human review, consent, and usable access are present.

concentration_pattern.value: early gains are expected to reach urban hubs, large firms, and highly skilled workers first, while rural communities, small businesses, and routine roles face greater disruption risk

sector_timing.value: finance and pharmaceuticals may experience effects sooner than agriculture and construction, with productivity gains lagging adoption as firms retool workflows and skills

gig_economy_tension.value: AI can connect freelancers to global clients while allowing one worker to perform the work of many, potentially compressing rates and raising insecurity

new_roles.value: data work, model safety, and data-center maintenance are identified as emerging areas alongside shrinking clerical and content tasks

observations.method: Regional economic and labor-market synthesis using country starting points, sector differences, AI-readiness comparisons, and gig-economy analysis.
observations.uncertainty: The report does not provide a single employment forecast or causal estimate; outcomes depend on adoption speed, skills, firm reorganization, competition, labor institutions, and public policy.
observations.subgroup: Routine workers, gig workers, informal workers, women in care and informal economies, rural workers, small firms, urban high-skill workers, and workers in sectors with different adoption lead times.
observations.counterinterpretation: AI may raise productivity and create new work, and late adopters may benefit if public infrastructure, skills, competition, and worker protections prevent gains from being captured by incumbents.

denominator.unit: reported policy pillars: put people first, govern innovation responsibly, and build future-ready systems

hard_levers.value: connectivity, devices, compute, data centers, power, and other physical foundations

soft_levers.value: skills, institutions, rules, competition, participation, and accountability

implementation_horizons.value: immediate 0-12 months, medium 1-2 years, and longer 3-5 years

governance_risks.value: bias, opacity, privacy, cybersecurity, surveillance, imported-model dependency, and weak public capacity can erode trust and rights

inclusion_measurement.value: the report calls for inclusion metrics, minimum standards, guardrails, and roadmaps tailored to different starting capacities

observations.method: Policy framework with capacity-tiered roadmaps and sector playbooks for health, education, finance, agriculture, cities, climate, public services, security, and justice.
observations.uncertainty: A roadmap or minimum standard does not establish implementation, financing, institutional ownership, or improved outcomes; capacity tiers can also simplify political and cultural differences within countries.
observations.subgroup: National and local governments, public-service users, civil society, firms, workers, communities with weak representation in data, and countries dependent on imported models or donor projects.
observations.counterinterpretation: Sequenced, locally adapted policy can turn AI into shared capability, but only if infrastructure investment is paired with public voice, rights protection, competition, and mechanisms for correction.

related_sources.claim: Official 130-page UNDP report PDF, including the people, economy, governance, and policy-roadmap chapters.
UNDP global Human Development Report 2025 context on AI, human choice, and development.

boundary: This record adds an AI-capability-to-divergence route across infrastructure, work, household security, public services, culture, gender, environment, and state capacity. It is not a causal country ranking, a respondent-level AI-use dataset, a forecast of aggregate inequality, or proof that any recommended safeguard has been implemented successfully.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official UNDP publication page and 130-page report PDF were reviewed for the Asia-Pacific frame, three transmission channels, distributional mechanisms, gender and environmental risks, nine background-paper foundation, and capacity-tiered policy recommendations.
